Its two heads give it a rich low-to-middle register; the sound is neither too sharp nor dull, but warm and resilient. By striking in different ways with the palm and the fingers the player gets several layers of sound, from a deep low drum tone to a crisp high one. Its resonance is like that of the conga, but the colour is softer and more Southeast Asian. The range is comparatively wide and it projects well, carrying clearly even outdoors. Compared with a Western drum kit it sounds gentler and more intimate; compared with a traditional Chinese drum it is more flexible and varied.

The instrument was originally called the saphon drum, and its development is closely tied to the Thai classical system, where it holds an important place in the wind-and-percussion ensemble known as the piphat. It is played in a distinctive way: the player uses the palms and the fingers of both hands on the two heads of the barrel-shaped body, producing a rich and varied sound. Over time the taphon became the drum most used in Thai folk music, and it appears widely in all kinds of traditional performance. Its influence is not confined to royal court music but reaches deep into folk culture. Today the taphon appears frequently in traditional music performances in Bangkok, Chiang Mai and other main cities; it is an important instrument for showing Thai cultural identity and still plays a part in contemporary practice.
